statement: Meridian's flag-conflict gate counts negated-verb pairs (skip/omit/avoid/disable + inflections) in the same polarity bucket as a bare NOT, so 'skip the rollout' and 'do not roll out' are treated as the same negative stance.
reason: Pre-fix, 'Skip the canary stage' vs 'Run the canary stage' produced no detected polarity flip -- 'skip' isn't a hand-coded negator and the object isn't an antonym pair -- so the gate silently let a real conflict through. Reproduced on the flag 'canary-required-for-prod' with two same-day writes from different reviewers.

statement: The polarity bucket for omission verbs must also cover 'defer' and 'postpone', not just 'skip'/'omit'/'avoid'/'disable'.
reason: A follow-up audit found 'defer the migration' vs 'run the migration now' scored as unrelated (LOW) instead of a real stance conflict -- same root cause as the original skip/omit gap, just a verb the first fix's word list didn't enumerate.

statement: Meridian's conflict judge must never trust a raw NLI contradiction score above 0.9 without a subject-overlap and polarity-agreement gate in front of it.
reason: The quantized cross-encoder over-fires on unrelated cross-topic pairs (>0.9) purely from surface phrasing similarity; a characterization test pins the two known false-fire pairs so a runtime bump can't silently reintroduce them.

statement: Meridian's structural comparator treats same-stance-different-scope as `coexist`, never `entailment`.
A free-text exception clause on a flag rule caps the conflict verdict at LOW unless the exception is structurally represented (its own scope object), never freeform prose.
Meridian's `recall()` grows its KNN search budget geometrically (starting at max(limit*8, 40), doubling on each pass) until it has `limit` in-scope active rows or has scanned the whole vector index.
reason: Audit finding: the vector index is global across every org/environment and rows are never deleted on revoke/supersede, so a fixed KNN budget could be entirely consumed by out-of-scope or inactive rows the post-filter discards, silently starving recall on an old, heavily-revised project.

statement: Embedding dimension is fixed at 384 the moment the vector table is created; changing embedding providers is a re-embed migration, never an in-place dimension change.
Meridian's `/why` route must search reasoned entries only -- a reason-less flag record can never win a rationale query.
reason: A reason-less row can't answer 'why', by construction: there's no text to cite. Searching it anyway just adds retrieval noise that can outscore the row that actually explains the decision.

statement: An empty result from Meridian's `/search` or `/why` never implies the environment holds no flags, so no route may report an environment as 'empty' on the basis of an empty result set.
reason: `/why` calling `recall(reasoned_only=True)` and getting zero hits back only tells you there are no REASONED rows above the relevance floor -- there could be dozens of reason-less flags still active. Conflating the two produced a false 'no flags configured' banner in the console for a project that had 40 active flags, none reasoned.

statement: Meridian's relevance floor for `/why` is 0.5; raising it to suppress low-confidence incorrect answers would need to exceed 0.88 and would also suppress a large share of genuinely correct ones.
reason: An internal calibration pass on labeled samples showed correct and incorrect hits clustering closely together in score, roughly 0.60-0.75 for both, so no single global cutoff cleanly separated the two without also losing good answers -- the fix had to look at what was matching, not just how confidently.

statement: Meridian's keyword rescue term (`kw`) is token-overlap fraction, weighted 0.3 against vector similarity's 0.7, specifically to rescue exact-token cases vector search alone misses.
The chunker used for the operator runbook importer can split an attribute from its keyword across a chunk boundary, which measurably hurts top-1 recall on short attribute/value rows.
reason: In a targeted replay of short key/value rows, a port number landed in the chunk AFTER the service name labeling it, so a query for the service name alone missed the port entirely -- top-1 recall on that replay only recovered once the window widened to recall@3. Table-aware chunking is the fix; not implemented yet.

statement: Meridian's `POST /flags/:id/resolve` route now maps a residual-conflict result to HTTP 409, mirroring `/flags` creation, instead of returning 200 with a 'resolved' body on an unresolved conflict.
reason: The earlier asymmetry meant a client branching on status code alone could silently ignore a real conflict, since only the body (not the status) signaled it. The CLI adapter was already coded to expect 409 here, so it degraded quietly for months.

statement: Every guarded write route accepts an audited `force_exception` override, except `/flags/:id/resolve`, which has no override at all -- its 409 is unconditional.
reason: Resolve is the terminal step of a review workflow; letting a client force through a real conflict at that exact step defeats the point of having a review workflow in the first place.

statement: A 400 (bad request) and a 401 (missing/invalid token) are evaluated BEFORE the monthly write-meter increments, so a malformed request never burns a metered write.

A guarded write must be metered only once it is known to actually run the conflict gate: `/flags/:id/resolve` pre-checks that `existing_id` resolves to an active flag before incrementing the monthly counter.
reason: Before the fix, the meter incremented atomically before the existence preflight, so a client typo in `existing_id` burned a monthly write unit for a request that never ran the gate at all -- contradicting the documented model that only gated attempts count.

statement: `GET /export` is open to every plan tier, not gated behind Pro/Team.
reason: Export is a data-portability guarantee, not a premium feature; gating it behind a paid tier would mean a free-tier operator can write flags they can't ever get back out in bulk.

statement: `GET /audit` is scoped to the caller's own org's writes and conflict events; there is no cross-org audit view at any plan tier.
Meridian's bearer-token check must use a constant-time comparison, never Python's plain string `==`.
reason: String equality short-circuits on the first mismatched byte, which is a textbook timing side-channel for a bearer token; `hmac.compare_digest` closes it for the cost of one import.

statement: `DEFAULT_ENVIRONMENT` is optional on every route above the flag-resolution layer, and its absence must produce a 400 with an explicit acceptance-criteria message, not a silent fallback.

Meridian's LLM-backed flag-description normalizer must FAIL CLOSED when the provider raises a connection error, timeout, 429, 5xx, or auth rejection -- refuse the write with a retryable 503, never silently skip the conflict check.
reason: The earlier behavior caught every provider exception and fell back to an all-unknown normalization, which stored the write with NO conflict check whenever the provider was merely unreachable -- a silent firewall bypass, not a graceful degrade.

statement: A PERMANENT provider client-error status (400 bad request, 404 unknown model, 422) must fail CLOSED too, mapped to a non-retryable 502 -- distinct from the retryable 503 class.
reason: Reproduced directly: a caller passing a bad model name got a 404 from the provider, which fell through to the SAME fail-open path as a merely-malformed reply, storing a write with no conflict check at all. A permanent rejection and 'the provider answered something we couldn't parse' are not the same failure class.

statement: Malformed model OUTPUT (2xx reply, no parseable JSON, or a refusal in prose) still degrades to an all-unknown normalization and fails OPEN -- distinct from the provider-error classes above, which fail closed.
reason: The provider answered successfully; it just didn't answer usefully. Refusing every write whenever the LLM declines to structure a description would make the reference text itself untrustworthy input, which isn't the threat model here.

statement: The normalizer's cache must use a unique temp file per write (`tempfile.mkstemp`), never a fixed `cache_path + '.tmp'`.
reason: Two threads racing a cache miss could both target the same tmp path; the loser's atomic rename then raised `FileNotFoundError` because the winner had already moved it. Reproduced with 8 concurrent threads pre-fix.

statement: Normalize happens OUTSIDE the store's write lock; only the DB read/write phase is scoped to the lock.
reason: Holding the lock across a 1-3s provider round-trip would head-of-line-block every other concurrent write for the duration of one slow LLM call.

statement: Meridian's multi-environment mode uses silo isolation: one SQLite file per environment, keyed by an opaque control-plane id, rather than a single pooled file scoped by a WHERE clause.
reason: Silo fits the single-writer SQLite engine: each environment becomes its own independent writer with no cross-environment lock contention, and isolation is by construction rather than by a WHERE clause a future migration could drop.

statement: The bounded threaded HTTP server (daemon threads, capped worker count) replaced the single-threaded server once concurrent multi-environment write load became routine.
reason: The single-threaded server's ~1-3s LLM normalizer call per guarded write stalled every other environment's request, including `/health` -- worth fixing before production load, not after an incident.

statement: A lease on an environment's own store MUST be released via a `finally` block once the request completes, so idle eviction or a concurrent environment delete can never close a connection still in use.
`registry.evict()` on a store that never drains must raise a `TimeoutError`, which the route maps to a clean 409 -- never force-close a store still leased by an in-flight request.
A request against an environment mid-delete must see `registry.get()` raise `LookupError` rather than hand out a lease on an entry that's draining toward close.
reason: That's a temporary condition (the environment is being torn down), not a broken store -- the route maps it to 503, not 500.

statement: Meridian's `role` field on an environment token is audit-only metadata at the engine layer; it grants no authorization on its own.
reason: grep across the route handlers shows zero authorization checks keyed on `role` anywhere -- every admin-only route is gated by the superadmin token alone. A self-hosted operator reading only the role table could reasonably assume otherwise, which is a doc gap, not an engine bug.

statement: Meridian's release script takes a backup, runs the full test suite, then builds and redeploys, gated by a health check with automatic rollback on failure.

The release script's health-gate rollback only covers the case where the new container fails its health check; it does NOT cover `docker run` itself failing (port already bound, env-file missing, daemon hiccup).
reason: Under `set -e` with no ERR trap, the old container is stopped and removed BEFORE the new one starts -- if `docker run` itself fails, the script dies with the old container gone and the new one never started, and the rollback tag sits unused.

statement: A same-minute retry after a failed release must not collide on the failed container's rename target.
reason: Timestamp resolution was minutes, not seconds; a same-minute retry's rename target collided with the previous failed container's name, and the fallback cleanup deleted the newest failed container -- the exact one an operator would want to debug.

statement: Claim-count verification during a release samples the count before and after and demands exact equality against a live, still-writable API.
reason: Any concurrent write during the build window is a false 'DATA RISK' alarm; the check is deliberately strict because a GENUINE mismatch (wrong volume mounted, count reset to zero) is exactly the failure mode a release gate exists to catch, even at the cost of occasional false alarms.

statement: The required CI test job does not build the Docker image or run the no-network boot test, so an image-only regression can merge green and first surface mid-release.
reason: Trade-off accepted, not fixed: a release gate that runs the full image build on every CI run would slow every PR down for a failure mode the release script's own gate already contains the blast radius of.

statement: Rollback image tags are pruned to the newest two, and pruning happens only after a health-gate rollback succeeds, never before.
Meridian's HTTP-concurrency tests must assert on a RELATIVE bound (an environment's measured non-blocking write time vs another environment's blocking one), never an absolute wall-clock ceiling.
reason: The absolute ceiling flaked on a starved 2-vCPU CI runner: `time.sleep` releases the GIL but the environment's post-sleep CPU work does not, so an absolute bound assumed dedicated cores the CI runner didn't actually have.

statement: A shared test-server-boot helper now lives in one conftest module; every fixture that boots a background HTTP server for a test delegates to it instead of copy-pasting the thread-start-and-wait mechanic.
reason: The same 'boot on a background thread, wait for readiness' mechanic was copy-pasted across a dozen test files with a too-tight timeout and no way to distinguish a real boot crash from a momentarily oversubscribed CI runner. One file's fix didn't fix the other eleven, because it was never one bug -- it was a dozen copies of the same one.

statement: A whitespace-only flag description passes truthiness validation, so it must be caught before it reaches the database CHECK constraint, not after.
reason: Letting the CHECK constraint reject it produced a 500 with raw schema-constraint text in the response body instead of a clean 400 -- an internal detail leaking into a client-facing error.

statement: Any provider-scoped cache key must be verified distinct across all supported providers, not just pairwise between the two most-used ones.
reason: A pairwise-only check passed while a third provider's key derivation still collided with one of the first two under a specific input -- only an all-pairs assertion would have caught it.

statement: A degrade-to-unknown-norm path must be exercised end-to-end with a refusing fake provider, not just unit-tested on the parser function in isolation.
Pin the conflict-judge runtime and its tokenizer library exactly; never unpin without re-running the labeled precision eval inside the built container first.
reason: The quantized judge model was found to shift its verdict on a fixed pair of near-duplicate sentences between two runtime/tokenizer combinations, flipping a case from a clear conflict to a clear non-conflict. Unpinned floors let every image build pull a different runtime than the eval was calibrated against.

statement: The MCP-style adapter's client library is pinned with `==`, not a floor, for the same reproducibility reason the conflict-judge runtime is pinned.
reason: A minor version bump in the adapter SDK can change tool-schema serialization or transport behavior; pinning means every deployment runs the exact combination the adapter's own test suite verified.

statement: Bump either pin deliberately, in its own change, with the full adapter test suite re-run -- never as a side effect of an unrelated dependency update.
Meridian must be positioned as guardrails for high-stakes, slow-changing configuration -- not a universal change-management platform.
reason: An internal realism eval showed genuine conflicts co-occur with unrelated changes constantly (most flag flips are routine, not policy-violating), so the conflict gate earns its keep only on the narrow slice of high-stakes flags, and positioning should say so rather than imply universal coverage.

statement: The conflict-detection feature is assessed as unproven on organic (non-test) usage, because no real operator write has yet triggered the gate outside of synthetic smoke tests.
reason: Lifetime detector record at time of assessment: two firings, both synthetic smoke-test plants, precision 1.00 but n=2 -- not enough organic signal to claim the gate demonstrably prevents real incidents yet, however sound the mechanism looks in isolation.

statement: Retraction (removing a wrong-at-birth flag record) and superseding (recording that a decision changed) are different operations and must never share a code path.
reason: Retract means the record should never have existed (typo, test junk, mis-scoped write) -- no new row, no why-chain link, required audit reason, and it cannot itself create a conflict. Supersede means the decision genuinely changed and the OLD decision's reasoning stays visible in the chain. Conflating them would either lose real history or pollute it with noise.

statement: Meridian's operator backups run via a daily scheduled job that calls the SQLite online-backup API inside the running container and copies each backup off-host afterward.
reason: The deployment previously had no off-host backups configured; the data lives in a named Docker volume, so an in-volume backup alone does not survive a volume or disk loss -- hence the separate off-host copy step.

statement: The container ships with no `sqlite3` CLI, so any backup or maintenance recipe must use the SQLite online-backup API (`conn.backup(dst)`) or a Python `VACUUM INTO` one-liner, never a shelled-out `sqlite3` command.
reason: Documentation once claimed a `docker exec ... sqlite3 ... VACUUM INTO` recipe matched what the nightly job actually ran; probing the live container confirmed `sqlite3` is absent and the job in fact uses the online-backup API, which needs neither a CLI nor a bare-connection assumption about virtual-table support.

statement: Recreating the deployment container must always pass the full canonical env-file, never a hand-assembled subset of variables.
reason: Container env is fixed at create time, so every upgrade does a stop-and-recreate and must re-pass every variable; hand-crafting the list risks silently dropping a model-cache path or a backup-path variable and losing offline model loading or a previously-cleared health warning.

statement: A rollback image tag is created before every mutating release step, and pruning of old rollback tags happens only after a successful health gate.
The pre-deploy off-host backup happens before any container mutation, never after.
reason: A backup taken after the mutation already happened can't roll back the mutation it was meant to protect against.

statement: Code changes to the deployment tooling are made in separate, disposable worktrees, never directly on the main checkout.
reason: The main checkout stays on a clean default branch as the orchestrator's read-only vantage point; each fix or feature gets an independent worktree so an in-progress change never blocks a concurrent one from being reviewed.

statement: The CI runner used for the release-gate test job is a persistent, self-hosted machine shared across jobs, not a fresh GitHub-hosted runner per run.
reason: A persistent runner lets the quantized-model cache survive between jobs, which matters for cold-start time, but it also means a job's state can leak into the next one if a test doesn't clean up after itself -- worth knowing before debugging a 'only fails in CI' flake.

statement: A throwaway container used to evaluate a new deploy platform must be destroyed once the evaluation is reviewed, never left running as a permanent fixture.
Every host-side script that mutates the live deployment must support a `--dry-run` flag that reports what it would do without mutating anything.
reason: A dry-run flag is what let an unattended nightly job safely report deployability (tests green, backup-baseline present) on every merge to the default branch without ever taking a live cutover action -- full unattended cutover stays behind an explicit manual gate.

statement: The engine's default bind address is 0.0.0.0 inside the container; the reverse proxy in front of it is what actually restricts what's publicly reachable.
A public bind with no bearer token configured must fail closed at boot, not start open with a logged warning.
reason: An operator who forgets to set the token on a publicly-reachable deployment previously got a running-but-wide-open API and a warning easy to miss in boot logs; failing the boot entirely makes the misconfiguration impossible to accidentally ship.

statement: The tunnel fronting the public API terminates at exactly two hostnames, both pointing at the same backend service.
reason: The product has one canonical domain and one legacy alias that predates the rename; both need to keep working, so the tunnel config and the server's own allowed-host check both list both names explicitly rather than assuming a single canonical host.

statement: A streamable-HTTP adapter transport must default to loopback-only; a proxy-fronted deployment that needs it to accept external connections must opt in explicitly with a host flag.
The `/health` route never probes the LLM normalizer, so a normalizer outage can leave guarded writes 503-ing while `/health` still reports green.
reason: A regional provider outage took the normalizer down for several hours; `/health` stayed green throughout because it only checks the store and embedder, not provider reachability, so the on-call operator had no automated signal and found out from a user report instead.

statement: A `/metrics` route exposing request counts and latency histograms is operator-only, gated the same way admin routes are.
The route label recorded in metrics is normalized against a fixed known-routes set before it ever reaches the metrics registry.
reason: The raw request path is attacker-controlled and every unmatched path already falls through to a 404, so recording it verbatim as a metrics label would let an attacker generate unbounded label cardinality just by requesting random paths.

statement: A cached normalizer-health check reports the wall-clock time of the last REAL probe, never advancing that timestamp on a cache hit.
reason: Reporting 'now' on a cached hit would tell a monitor the write path was just verified when the underlying probe may be up to the cache TTL stale -- the `cached` flag alone doesn't convey that staleness on its own.

statement: A throwaway LXC container was used to evaluate an alternative deploy platform before deciding whether to adopt it for the main deployment.
reason: Testing against a disposable box first, exactly like every other infra evaluation, avoids risking the live deployment on a platform that might not pan out.

statement: A locally-hosted LLM was evaluated as a normalizer backend and found unsuitable for sustained production load, despite working fine on cold/warm single calls.
reason: The shared GPU host saturated under sustained request volume -- warm-up performance was fine, but the host wedged after a few hundred consecutive calls while keeping the model loaded and admin endpoints alive, a known queueing pathology under this workload shape.

statement: A remote LLM proxy is production-shaped in a way a directly-hosted local model, sharing a GPU with other workloads, is not.
reason: A same-day head-to-head comparison: the remote proxy sustained full throughput with zero failures at the same per-call latency, while the local shared-GPU host wedged partway through an equivalent run.
